newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia July trade gap as expected, say economists.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia July trade gap as expected, say economists.

text.p: Malaysia's announcement of a 624.5 million ringgit ($250.80 million) trade deficit for July after a surplus of 551.4 million in June was in line with market expectations, economists said on Monday.
They said the deficit figure pointed to a more sustainable trend evolving after the data for the first six months showed a dramatic improvement over the previous year.

"The figure is in line with our own expectations. This is a return to a more sustainable trend, following the previous two months' surpluses," said Desmond Supple, an economist with research consultancy I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
Malaysia's Statistics Department said in the first seven months of the year the trade gap was 1.4 billion ringgit against 6.9 billion in the year-ago period.

"That is a very big improvement over last year. If you annualise it for the whole year, and if the same trend continues, we expect the trade deficit to be around 2.5 billion ringgit for the year," said Ghazali Atan, economist with MBf Unit Trust Management in Kuala Lumpur.
This compares with a gap of 9.2 billion ringgit last year.
Most economists have lowered their full year forecast for the country's trade deficit after a low first half figure.

In a poll by Reuters last week, economists from nine research houses said the trade deficit in 1996 would be an average 4.95 billion ringgit against an average 8.55 billion they had predicted in a poll three months ago.
Economists said the high deficit figure in July was due to a slowdown in exports, both manufactured and commodity, and an increase in some large, one-time equipment imports not accounted for earlier.
Bulky imports in the first seven months of 1996 declined by 30.7 percent, or 1.7 billion ringgit, to 3.9 billion against 5.7 billion in the same period in 1995.

"What these figures suggest is some of those lumpy import items are yet to impact on the trade figures, so the average monthly deficit should be around this figure over the rest of the year," Supple of I.D.E.A. said.

The economists, many of whom had last year expressed worries that the fast-growing Malaysian economy was overheating, said that while they were happy with an economic slowdown, the slowing export growth was cause for concern.
Nik Ahmad Fauzan, economist with Vickers Ballas in Kuala Lumpur, said while the overall figures were improving, year-on-year export growth at just 2.5 percent was low.
"On the whole the numbers are disappointing. I was hoping for export growth of around five percent, but it actually came out roughly half of that," he said.

The economists said the ringgit's appreciation against the yen, increased gains from petroleum exports and a rise in export of electronic goods despite a worldwide slump, had helped improve the country's balance of payments in the first six months.
"Basically, we are just being fortunate. This (weak yen) has allowed us to do quite well despite the electronic sector being hit by some slowdown," Ghazali of MBf said.
"For the whole year the trend is quite optimstic. It will be helpful in reducing people's doubts about the current account deficit and prospects for the ringgit," Ghazali said.
